claim: During mitosis, kinetochore-attached microtubules form bundles (k-fibers) in which many filaments grow and shorten in near-perfect unison to align and segregate each chromosome.
source: During mitosis, kinetochore-attached microtubules form bundles (k-fibers) in which many filaments grow and shorten in near-perfect unison to align and segregate each chromosome.
evidence: This is a general statement about mitotic spindle behavior that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Individual microtubules grow at intrinsically variable rates.
source: However, individual microtubules grow at intrinsically variable rates, which must be tightly regulated for a k-fiber to behave as a single unit.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1a and cited literature.

claim: Microtubule pairs growing in vitro are coordinated by mechanical coupling.
source: Here, we use a novel dual laser trap assay to show that microtubule pairs growing in vitro are coordinated by mechanical coupling.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the dual laser trap assay presented in the manuscript.

claim: Microtubule growth is interrupted by stochastic, force-dependent pauses.
source: Kinetic analyses show that microtubule growth is interrupted by stochastic, force-dependent pauses and indicate persistent heterogeneity in growth speed during non-pauses.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic analysis of force-clamp data presented in Figure 5.

claim: There is persistent heterogeneity in growth speed during non-pauses.
source: Kinetic analyses show that microtubule growth is interrupted by stochastic, force-dependent pauses and indicate persistent heterogeneity in growth speed during non-pauses.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of microtubule growth data.

claim: A simple model incorporating both force-dependent pausing and persistent growth speed heterogeneity explains the measured coordination of microtubule pairs without any free fit parameters.
source: A simple model incorporating both force-dependent pausing and persistent growth speed heterogeneity explains the measured coordination of microtubule pairs without any free fit parameters.
evidence: This claim is supported by the modeling results presented in Figure 6 and comparison with experimental data.

claim: Human RPE1 cells have 10–15 microtubules per k-fiber.
source: The number of microtubules per k-fiber varies across species; human RPE1 cells have 10–15 microtubules per k-fiber, while marsupial PTK2 cells have more than 20, and cervid Indian Muntjac cells have up to 60 (O'Toole et al., 2020; Drpic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Marsupial PTK2 cells have more than 20 microtubules per k-fiber.
source: The number of microtubules per k-fiber varies across species; human RPE1 cells have 10–15 microtubules per k-fiber, while marsupial PTK2 cells have more than 20, and cervid Indian Muntjac cells have up to 60 (O'Toole et al., 2020; Drpic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cervid Indian Muntjac cells have up to 60 microtubules per k-fiber.
source: The number of microtubules per k-fiber varies across species; human RPE1 cells have 10–15 microtubules per k-fiber, while marsupial PTK2 cells have more than 20, and cervid Indian Muntjac cells have up to 60 (O'Toole et al., 2020; Drpic et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Budding yeast have just a single microtubule per kinetochore.
source: Budding yeast lack k-fiber bundles, having just a single microtubule per kinetochore (Winey et al., 1995), although microtubules attached to sister kinetochores on opposite sides of the yeast spindle must still coordinate with each other.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Kinetochore-attached tips within a single k-fiber remain very close to one another (within ~0.2 µm along the bundle axis).
source: Kinetochore-attached tips within a single k-fiber remain very close to one another (within ~0.2 µm along the bundle axis) (O'Toole et al., 2020) even as the bundle grows and shortens (Cimini et al., 2004) by the addition and loss of tubulin subunits at each tip (Maddox et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Microtubule growth speed varies considerably in purified tubulin systems.
source: Microtubule growth speed varies considerably in purified tubulin systems (Figure 1a; Cleary et al., 2022; Gildersleeve et al., 1992; Mahserejian et al., 2022), in cell extracts (Geisterfer et al., 2020), and in live cells (Cassimeris et al., 1988; Gaudenz et al., 2010; Yamashita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a and citations to published literature.

claim: Microtubule growth speed varies considerably in cell extracts.
source: Microtubule growth speed varies considerably in purified tubulin systems (Figure 1a; Cleary et al., 2022; Gildersleeve et al., 1992; Mahserejian et al., 2022), in cell extracts (Geisterfer et al., 2020), and in live cells (Cassimeris et al., 1988; Gaudenz et al., 2010; Yamashita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Microtubule growth speed varies considerably in live cells.
source: Microtubule growth speed varies considerably in purified tubulin systems (Figure 1a; Cleary et al., 2022; Gildersleeve et al., 1992; Mahserejian et al., 2022), in cell extracts (Geisterfer et al., 2020), and in live cells (Cassimeris et al., 1988; Gaudenz et al., 2010; Yamashita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Part of microtubule growth heterogeneity can be attributed to pausing, when microtubules stochastically stop and start growing during periods of net growth.
source: Part of this heterogeneity can be attributed to pausing, when microtubules stochastically stop and start growing during periods of net growth (Amoah-Darko and White, 2022; Mahserejian et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tension applied to individual microtubules in vitro biases them toward growth.
source: Tension applied to individual microtubules in vitro biases them toward growth (Figure 1a; Akiyoshi et al., 2010), while compression biases them toward shortening (Dogterom and Yurke, 1997; Janson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1a and citations to published literature.

claim: Compression biases microtubules toward shortening.
source: Tension applied to individual microtubules in vitro biases them toward growth (Figure 1a; Akiyoshi et al., 2010), while compression biases them toward shortening (Dogterom and Yurke, 1997; Janson et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mechanical effects should promote synchronization of any group of microtubules whose tips are all coupled to the same load.
source: Theoretically, these mechanical effects should promote synchronization of any group of microtubules whose tips, like the tips of kinetochore-attached microtubules within a k-fiber, are all coupled to the same load (Banigan et al., 2015; Schwietert and Kierfeld, 2020; Skibbens et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is based on theoretical work cited from published literature.

claim: When microtubule pairs are mechanically coupled to a single load through a material of sufficient stiffness, their growth is tightly coordinated.
source: We show that when microtubule pairs are mechanically coupled to a single load through a material of sufficient stiffness, their growth is tightly coordinated.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the dual-trap assay.

claim: Pausing during microtubule growth is suppressed by tension.
source: By re-analyzing recordings of individual microtubules growing under constant force (from Akiyoshi et al., 2010) and examining their stochastic pausing kinetics, we show that pausing is suppressed by tension.
evidence: This claim is supported by re-analysis of published data presented in Figure 5.

claim: When coupled through soft springs (κ=1 pN·µm–1), microtubule pairs tended to grow at different rates and their tips often became separated by more than a micrometer.
source: When coupled through soft springs (κ=1 pN·µm–1), microtubule pairs tended to grow at different rates and their tips often became separated by more than a micrometer (Figure 3a, left, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average tip separation for soft-coupled pairs after 300 s was 0.8±0.2 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10 pairs).
source: After 300 s, the average tip separation for soft-coupled pairs grew to 0.8±0.2 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10 pairs) (Figure 3b, left).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3b.

claim: When coupled through stiff springs (κ=5 pN·µm–1), growth speeds were better matched, and the microtubule tips remained closer together.
source: When coupled through stiff springs (κ=5 pN·µm–1), growth speeds were better matched, and the microtubule tips remained closer together (Figure 3a, right, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, right).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The average tip separation for stiff-coupled pairs after 300 s was 0.25±0.06 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10 pairs).
source: The average tip separation for stiff-coupled pairs after 300 s was 0.25±0.06 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10 pairs) (Figure 3b, right), significantly lower than for soft-coupled pairs (p=0.03 based on a Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney two sample rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 3b with statistical analysis.

claim: The average tip separation for stiff-coupled pairs was significantly lower than for soft-coupled pairs (p=0.03).
source: The average tip separation for stiff-coupled pairs after 300 s was 0.25±0.06 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10 pairs) (Figure 3b, right), significantly lower than for soft-coupled pairs (p=0.03 based on a Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney two sample rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: During the first 100 s of growth, the average rate of tip separation for soft-coupled pairs was 0.23±0.04 µm·min–1 (mean ± SEM from N=23 pairs).
source: During the first 100 s of growth, the average rate of tip separation for soft-coupled pairs was 0.23±0.04 µm·min–1 (mean ± SEM from N=23 pairs), while the average rate of tip separation for stiff-coupled pairs was only 0.14±0.02 µm·min–1 (mean ± SEM from N=26 pairs; p=0.03 based on a Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney two sample rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements.

claim: During the first 100 s of growth, the average rate of tip separation for stiff-coupled pairs was 0.14±0.02 µm·min–1 (mean ± SEM from N=26 pairs).
source: During the first 100 s of growth, the average rate of tip separation for soft-coupled pairs was 0.23±0.04 µm·min–1 (mean ± SEM from N=23 pairs), while the average rate of tip separation for stiff-coupled pairs was only 0.14±0.02 µm·min–1 (mean ± SEM from N=26 pairs; p=0.03 based on a Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney two sample rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements with statistical analysis.

claim: Stiff-coupled microtubule pairs were much less likely to exceed a separation of 0.8 µm than their soft-coupled counterparts (p=0.01).
source: Consistent with their lower average tip separation, stiff-coupled microtubule pairs were much less likely to exceed a separation of 0.8 µm than their soft-coupled counterparts (p=0.01, log-rank test; Figure 3c), which sometimes separated by 0.8 µm in as little as 60 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: After 400 s, more than 80% of the stiff-coupled pairs had tip separations that remained below 0.8 µm.
source: Even after 400 s, more than 80% of the stiff-coupled pairs had tip separations that remained below 0.8 µm, while fewer than half of the soft-coupled pairs had tip separations below 0.8 µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data.

claim: After 400 s, fewer than half of the soft-coupled pairs had tip separations below 0.8 µm.
source: Even after 400 s, more than 80% of the stiff-coupled pairs had tip separations that remained below 0.8 µm, while fewer than half of the soft-coupled pairs had tip separations below 0.8 µm.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data.

claim: Mean growth speed increases exponentially with applied tension.
source: When averaged across time and across many individual microtubules, mean growth speed increases exponentially with applied tension (Akiyoshi et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Tension delays pause entry and accelerates pause exit.
source: This analysis revealed that tension delays pause entry and accelerates pause exit (Figure 5a).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of force-clamp data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The average growth speed during runs was accelerated by tension.
source: In addition, the average growth speed during runs was accelerated by tension (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: All three rates (pause entry, pause exit, and average growth speed during runs) were well-fit by single exponential functions of force.
source: All three rates, pause entry, pause exit, and average growth speed during runs, were well-fit by single exponential functions of force (Figure 5; see Table 1 for fit parameters).
evidence: This claim is supported by curve fitting to experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The pausing model of microtubule growth provided significantly better fits to dual-trap data than the non-pausing model.
source: The pausing model of microtubule growth provided significantly better fits to our dual-trap data than the non-pausing model.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model predictions to experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: After 300 s, the average tip separation for simulated soft-coupled pairs was 0.79±0.01 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10,000 simulations).
source: After 300 s, the average tip separation for simulated soft-coupled pairs grew to 0.79±0.01 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10,000 simulations), while simulated stiff-coupled pairs had a lower average tip separation of 0.43±0.005 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10,000 simulations; Figure 6b), similar to the corresponding separations measured in dual-trap experiments (0.8±0.2 µm and 0.25±0.06 µm, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6b.

claim: After 300 s, simulated stiff-coupled pairs had a lower average tip separation of 0.43±0.005 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10,000 simulations).
source: After 300 s, the average tip separation for simulated soft-coupled pairs grew to 0.79±0.01 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10,000 simulations), while simulated stiff-coupled pairs had a lower average tip separation of 0.43±0.005 µm (mean ± SEM from N=10,000 simulations; Figure 6b), similar to the corresponding separations measured in dual-trap experiments (0.8±0.2 µm and 0.25±0.06 µm, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Mechanical coupling coordinates microtubule growth in at least two distinct ways: first, by counteracting persistent (intrinsic) differences in microtubule growth speed, and second, by selectively suppressing stochastic pausing in the lagging tip relative to the leading tip.
source: Overall, the strong agreement between the pausing model and the dual-trap recordings suggests that mechanical coupling coordinates microtubule growth in at least two distinct ways: first, by counteracting persistent (intrinsic) differences in microtubule growth speed, and second, by selectively suppressing stochastic pausing in the lagging tip relative to the leading tip.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the success of the pausing model in explaining experimental data.

claim: Pairs of microtubule tips growing in vitro are kept in close proximity when sharing a single load through a coupling material of sufficient stiffness.
source: Using our dual-trap assay, we found that pairs of microtubule tips growing in vitro are kept in close proximity when sharing a single load through a coupling material of sufficient stiffness.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary experimental finding.

claim: Tip pairs in the experiments were kept within a fraction of a micrometer by couplers of only κ=5 pN·µm–1.
source: Tip pairs in our experiments were kept within a fraction of a micrometer by couplers of only κ=5 pN·µm–1, a modest stiffness within the ranges reported for elements of the kinetochore (Schwietert et al., 2022; Volkov et al., 2018), pericentromeric chromatin (Chacón et al., 2014), and mitotic chromosomes (Nicklas, 1983; Poirier et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and comparison to published literature.

claim: The kinetochore and its underlying centromeric chromatin both appear to deform together to maintain close contacts with k-fiber plus-ends in vivo.
source: Because the kinetochore and its underlying centromeric chromatin both appear to deform together to maintain close contacts with k-fiber plus-ends in vivo (O'Toole et al., 2020), the plus-ends presumably exert forces on each other through a composite material composed of both kinetochore and chromatin.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mechanical coupling is a major coordinating influence on plus-end growth dynamics within k-fiber bundles.
source: We propose that this mechanical coupling is a major coordinating influence on plus-end growth dynamics within k-fiber bundles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and modeling results.

claim: Tension reduced the rate at which growing tips entered a pause state.
source: More specifically, tension reduced the rate at which growing tips entered a pause state.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of force-clamp data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Tension increased the rate at which paused tips resumed growth.
source: Tension also increased the rate at which paused tips resumed growth, which implies that pause exit is associated with movement toward the plus-end, in the same direction as the applied force and therefore assisted by the force.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of force-clamp data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Pause entry is associated with movement of tension-bearing elements at the tip toward the minus end, opposite the direction of applied force and therefore inhibited by the force.
source: This finding implies that pause entry is associated with movement of tension-bearing elements at the tip toward the minus end, opposite the direction of applied force and therefore inhibited by the force.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed force-dependence of pause entry.

claim: Pause exit is associated with movement toward the plus-end, in the same direction as the applied force and therefore assisted by the force.
source: Tension also increased the rate at which paused tips resumed growth, which implies that pause exit is associated with movement toward the plus-end, in the same direction as the applied force and therefore assisted by the force.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed force-dependence of pause exit.

claim: Pauses occur because the configuration of the growing microtubule tip fluctuates and sometimes becomes transiently refractory to the incorporation of new tubulin subunits.
source: Presumably, these pauses occur because the configuration of the growing microtubule tip fluctuates and sometimes becomes transiently refractory to the incorporation of new tubulin subunits (Cleary and Hancock, 2021; Mahserejian et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Tension could help straighten curved structures at the microtubule tip, thereby accelerating lateral bond formation and favoring growth.
source: Tension could help straighten these curved structures, thereby accelerating lateral bond formation and favoring growth (Cleary and Hancock, 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The necessity of including microtubules with different intrinsic growth speeds for the model's success implies structural heterogeneity in the growing tips that must persist for many minutes.
source: The necessity of including microtubules with different intrinsic growth speeds for our model's success implies structural heterogeneity in the growing tips that must persist for many minutes, even as thousands of tubulin subunits are being added.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Persistent differences in microtubule growth speed might arise from different or mismatched protofilament numbers.
source: In principle, these persistent differences might arise from different or mismatched protofilament numbers (Chrétien et al., 1992; Rai et al., 2021) or the accumulation of other lattice defects (Wieczorek et al., 2015) that result in varying degrees of tip taper (Coombes et al., 2013; or tip 'raggedness' Brouhard and Rice, 2018) which are more or less conducive to microtubule growth.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Persistent differences in microtubule growth speed might arise from the accumulation of lattice defects.
source: In principle, these persistent differences might arise from different or mismatched protofilament numbers (Chrétien et al., 1992; Rai et al., 2021) or the accumulation of other lattice defects (Wieczorek et al., 2015) that result in varying degrees of tip taper (Coombes et al., 2013; or tip 'raggedness' Brouhard and Rice, 2018) which are more or less conducive to microtubule growth.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mechanical coupling is a feasible mechanism that could coordinate k-fiber microtubules and maintain their synchronous growth in the mitotic spindle.
source: Overall, our work demonstrates that mechanical coupling is a feasible mechanism that could coordinate k-fiber microtubules and maintain their synchronous growth in the mitotic spindle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The dual-trap assay uses two separate laser trapping microscopes located adjacent to one another in the same room and connected to a single computer.
source: Our new dual-trap assay uses two separate laser trapping microscopes, located adjacent to one another in the same room and connected to a single computer.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: The computer simultaneously monitors and controls the forces on both microtubules in the dual-trap assay.
source: The computer then simultaneously monitors and controls the forces on both microtubules.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: Forces in the dual-trap feedback system are updated at a rate of 50 Hz.
source: Forces in our dual-trap feedback system are updated at a rate of 50 Hz, which is more than sufficient for accurately simulating the elastic coupling between two microtubules (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method with reference to supporting data.

claim: Each microtubule generally experiences between 1 and 7 pN of tension in the dual-trap experiments.
source: Thus, each microtubule generally experiences between 1 and 7 pN of tension, close to the estimated average of 4–6 pN experienced by kinetochore-microtubules in budding yeast (Chacón et al., 2014; Parmar et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a description of experimental conditions with comparison to published estimates.

claim: The estimated average tension experienced by kinetochore-microtubules in budding yeast is 4–6 pN.
source: Thus, each microtubule generally experiences between 1 and 7 pN of tension, close to the estimated average of 4–6 pN experienced by kinetochore-microtubules in budding yeast (Chacón et al., 2014; Parmar et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Distributions of run and pause durations were approximately exponential.
source: Distributions of run and pause durations were approximately exponential (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), consistent with a relatively simple two-state kinetic model of microtubule growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), in which pause entry and exit are considered Poisson processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The exponential distributions of run and pause durations are consistent with a two-state kinetic model in which pause entry and exit are considered Poisson processes.
source: Distributions of run and pause durations were approximately exponential (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), consistent with a relatively simple two-state kinetic model of microtubule growth (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a), in which pause entry and exit are considered Poisson processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed distributions.

claim: The non-pausing model could not explain the behavior of microtubule pairs measured in the dual-trap assay.
source: Despite its direct derivation from force-clamp data, the non-pausing model could not explain the behavior of microtubule pairs measured in the dual-trap assay (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model predictions to experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Simulated microtubule pairs using the non-pausing model developed much larger tip separations than real microtubule pairs over time.
source: Simulated microtubule pairs developed much larger tip separations than real microtubule pairs over time, implying that this model overestimates real microtubule variability.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental data.

claim: The non-pausing model overestimates real microtubule variability.
source: Simulated microtubule pairs developed much larger tip separations than real microtubule pairs over time, implying that this model overestimates real microtubule variability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of model predictions to experimental data.

claim: The non-pausing model does not capture the degree to which real microtubules are coordinated by mechanical coupling.
source: The simulated microtubule pairs showed especially poor agreement with real microtubule pairs under the stiff-coupled condition (Figure 4c, red curves), indicating that the non-pausing model also does not capture the degree to which real microtubules are coordinated by mechanical coupling.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of model predictions to experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The pausing model scored better than the non-pausing model when using probability to compare simulated to in vitro measurements.
source: In addition, the pausing model scored better than the non-pausing model when we used probability to compare simulated to in vitro measurements (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Stochastic pausing alone is insufficient to generate the large and persistent differences in growth speed exhibited by real microtubules.
source: The low variability predicted by this model (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), particularly under the soft-coupled condition, indicates that stochastic pausing alone is insufficient to generate the large and persistent differences in growth speed exhibited by real microtubules).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparison of the ergodic pausing model to experimental data.

claim: Kinetochore-decorated beads track with microtubule plus-ends under tensions between 0.5 and 18 pN.
source: The bead positions served as accurate proxies for the microtubule tip positions because kinetochore-decorated beads are known to track with microtubule plus-ends under tensions between 0.5 and 18 pN (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Asbury et al., 2006; Franck et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2016; Powers et al., 2009; Tien et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Yeast kinetochores are very small, only ~130 nm in length.
source: In addition, the yeast kinetochores used to link the beads to the microtubule tips are very small, only ~130 nm in length (Gonen et al., 2012), compared to the relevant micrometer-scale tip displacements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The small size of the yeast kinetochore ensures that its (visco)elastic properties did not significantly affect experimental results.
source: The small size of the yeast kinetochore, as well as the slow change in force on each tip (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), ensures that the kinetochore's (visco)elastic properties did not significantly affect experimental results, because any force-dependent changes in its length had a negligible effect compared to tip growth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetochore size and experimental observations.

claim: Mechanical coupling could account for the rapid, sub-micron responses required to coordinate microtubule tips within a k-fiber.
source: Therefore, mechanical coupling could account for the rapid, sub-micron responses required to coordinate microtubule tips within a k-fiber, while microtubule-modifiers and spindle-wide phenomena, like polar ejection forces and poleward flux, are likely to help set overall k-fiber length (Risteski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and comparison to other mechanisms.

claim: Microtubule-modifiers and spindle-wide phenomena are likely to help set overall k-fiber length.
source: Therefore, mechanical coupling could account for the rapid, sub-micron responses required to coordinate microtubule tips within a k-fiber, while microtubule-modifiers and spindle-wide phenomena, like polar ejection forces and poleward flux, are likely to help set overall k-fiber length (Risteski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mechanical forces would be transmitted essentially instantaneously between neighboring tips through local deformations of the material through which the tips are coupled.
source: On the other hand, mechanical forces would be transmitted essentially instantaneously between neighboring tips through local deformations of the material through which the tips are coupled.
evidence: This is based on physical principles of force transmission through elastic materials.

claim: It is unclear whether selective enrichment of microtubule-regulating proteins is sufficient to explain the very tight coordination across many individual microtubule tips within a k-fiber.
source: However, whether such selective enrichment is sufficient to explain the very tight coordination across many individual microtubule tips within a k-fiber is unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current understanding.

claim: The localization of some microtubule regulators is enriched near kinetochores specifically when a kinetochore is moving anti-poleward and its k-fiber is growing longer.
source: The localization of some of these regulators is enriched near kinetochores specifically when a kinetochore is moving anti-poleward and its k-fiber is growing longer (Amaro et al., 2010; Castrogiovanni et al., 2022; Tirnauer et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Many microtubule-associated proteins that regulate growth in vitro are implicated in modulating k-fiber dynamics and kinetochore movements in cells.
source: Many microtubule-associated proteins that are known to regulate growth in vitro are implicated in modulating k-fiber dynamics and kinetochore movements in cells, including TOG-family proteins such as XMAP215 (Brouhard et al., 2008) and CLASP (Al-Bassam et al., 2010; Maiato et al., 2003a; Sousa et al., 2007), mitotic kinesins such as MCAK and Kif18A (Sanhaji et al., 2011; Stumpff et al., 2012), and other plus-end-trackers such as EB1 (reviewed in Amin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Modest perturbations of kinetochore-attached microtubule dynamics can lead to chromosome mis-segregation.
source: Uncovering how microtubule tips maintain a high degree of synchrony within k-fibers of up to 60 microtubules is critical to understanding how chromosomes are accurately segregated during normal mitosis and why even modest perturbations of kinetochore-attached microtubule dynamics can lead to mis-segregation (Bakhoum and Compton, 2012; Bakhoum et al., 2009; Ertych et al., 2014; Stumpff et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Microtubule tips exhibit highly variable growth speeds and switch stochastically between distinct states of growth and shortening.
source: The tightly coordinated growth of microtubules within a k-fiber bundle is remarkable because individually, microtubule tips exhibit highly variable growth speeds and switch stochastically between distinct states of growth and shortening (Brouhard, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: K-fiber bundles are usually under tension, not compression.
source: Compressive forces can cause a bundle of microtubules growing in vitro to switch cooperatively into a shortening state (Laan et al., 2008), but k-fiber bundles are usually under tension, not compression (Khodjakov and Rieder, 1996; Waters et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Compressive forces can cause a bundle of microtubules growing in vitro to switch cooperatively into a shortening state.
source: Compressive forces can cause a bundle of microtubules growing in vitro to switch cooperatively into a shortening state (Laan et al., 2008), but k-fiber bundles are usually under tension, not compression (Khodjakov and Rieder, 1996; Waters et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mechanical coupling was proposed decades ago as an explanation for coordination between sister k-fibers.
source: Mechanical coupling was proposed decades ago as an explanation for coordination between sister k-fibers (Gardner et al., 2005; Khodjakov et al., 1996; Skibbens et al., 1995; Skibbens et al., 1993; Wan et al., 2012), but how effectively it can coordinate microtubules within a k-fiber has not been determined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: How effectively mechanical coupling can coordinate microtubules within a k-fiber has not been determined prior to this work.
source: Mechanical coupling was proposed decades ago as an explanation for coordination between sister k-fibers (Gardner et al., 2005; Khodjakov et al., 1996; Skibbens et al., 1995; Skibbens et al., 1993; Wan et al., 2012), but how effectively it can coordinate microtubules within a k-fiber has not been determined.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that this work addresses.

claim: Previous theoretical studies have generally neglected any differences in growth speed between microtubules.
source: However, these studies have generally neglected any differences in growth speed between microtubules and therefore cannot address how much variability exists, nor how such variability is suppressed.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of prior theoretical work.

claim: The possibility that part of microtubule growth variability can be attributed to tension-dependent pausing has not been explored in previous theoretical studies.
source: Furthermore, to our knowledge, the possibility that part of this variability (and suppression thereof) can be attributed to tension-dependent pausing during microtubule growth has not been explored.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in prior theoretical work.
